concepts.decision: Harden configuration/identity/management, inventory lifecycle, monitor health, and control changes for each component role.
concepts.definition: Devices and services such as switches, routers, firewalls, access points, controllers, and supporting hardware that forward, enforce, or manage connectivity.
concepts.failureExample: Default credentials on a network controller override sound downstream segmentation.
concepts.label: Network Components

concepts.decision: Choose/protect medium from location, threat, capacity, propagation quality, maintainability, and inspection needs.
concepts.definition: Physical paths—copper, fiber, radio, and related infrastructure—that carry signals with different tamper, interception, distance, attenuation, and interference properties.
concepts.failureExample: A cable run through public space is tapped despite strong application encryption metadata exposure.
concepts.label: Transmission Media

concepts.decision: Set policy and remediation/quarantine paths; reassess posture and log the admission decision.
concepts.definition: Admission control using identity, device posture, location, role, certificate, and risk to allow, restrict, redirect, or quarantine network access.
concepts.failureExample: A device passes NAC then becomes compromised after admission.
concepts.label: Network Access Control

concepts.decision: Apply and monitor controls after admission, with device lifecycle/identity ownership and incident containment.
concepts.definition: Host controls such as hardened configuration, EDR, host firewall, encryption, patching, integrity, logging, and response.
concepts.failureExample: A compliant laptop loses patches and is exploited while still on its permitted VLAN.
concepts.label: Endpoint Security

concepts.decision: Verify independence across power, conduit, provider, controller, firmware, identity, and failover behavior.
concepts.definition: Multiple components or paths intended to preserve service through a failure.
concepts.failureExample: Two links share one conduit or control plane and fail together during an outage.
concepts.label: Redundancy

concepts.decision: Track support status and replace/compensate for unsupported hardware/firmware before exposure becomes unfixable.
concepts.definition: Vendor support, warranty, maintenance, inventory, replacement, patch, and retirement management for network assets.
concepts.failureExample: An unsupported switch cannot receive a fix for a critical management-plane flaw.
concepts.label: Support Lifecycle

misconceptions.claim: A switch or router is secure once its default password changes.
misconceptions.correction: Secure operation also requires hardened services, updates, management-path protection, physical security, backups, monitoring, and support.

outcome: Evaluate a network component or endpoint and select controls for operation, media, access admission, maintenance, and failure conditions.

sections.body: Infrastructure operation includes secure configuration, redundant power and paths, environmental protection, maintenance, warranty, support, inventory, and replacement planning. Transmission media require physical protection against tampering and interception plus attention to propagation quality, attenuation, interference, and signal integrity. The control choice depends on location, threat, availability requirement, and whether the medium can be inspected or replaced.
keyPoints: Redundancy improves availability but can duplicate failure or misconfiguration if not tested.
Media security includes physical route, termination points, shielding, and monitoring.
Unsupported components create security and recovery risk even when configuration is correct.
sections.title: Protect the infrastructure and its medium

sections.body: Network Access Control can combine identity, device posture, location, authorization, and quarantine to decide whether a device joins a network or receives a segment. Host-based controls such as hardened configurations, endpoint protection, host firewalls, encryption, patching, EDR, and logging reinforce network policy. NAC is not a replacement for endpoint security: a compliant device can still be compromised after admission.
keyPoints: NAC decisions should be explicit about identity, posture, scope, and remediation.
Physical and virtual access-control solutions must cover relevant entry points.
Endpoint telemetry should feed D7 monitoring and incident processes.
sections.title: Admit and protect endpoints deliberately

sections.body: Infrastructure operation includes power redundancy, environmental and physical protection, warranty and support status, spare capacity, maintenance windows, configuration baselines, and tested failover. Transmission media choices require physical security, separation, shielding, distance, attenuation, interference, signal propagation, tamper evidence, and monitoring. A redundant path that shares a conduit, power source, provider, or unsupported firmware may fail together.
keyPoints: Support and warranty are security inputs because unavailable fixes and replacement capacity extend exposure.
Media quality affects availability, observability, and integrity assumptions.
Record common-mode dependencies when claiming resilience.
sections.title: Operate infrastructure and transmission media safely

sections.body: Network Access Control can be physical or virtual and may evaluate identity, device posture, location, certificate, role, and current risk before allowing, restricting, redirecting, or quarantining a connection. Host-based endpoint controls then enforce local configuration, malware prevention, firewall, integrity, logging, patch, and response requirements. NAC is an admission decision, not proof that a host remains safe after connection.
keyPoints: Physical NAC can control port or switch placement; virtual NAC can mediate overlays, cloud, or software-defined access.
Posture signals need freshness, trust, and exception handling.
Endpoint controls must continue after admission and support isolation or recovery.
sections.title: Gate admission and harden endpoints

summary: Network security depends on the physical medium, infrastructure lifecycle, admission decisions, and host controls that implement the architecture.

assumptions: Only entities and claims anchored in the canonical unit or explicitly labeled hypothetical scenario are used.
A highlighted path means the learner is inspecting that path; it does not assert the event occurred.
The current source is authoritative for facts; this treatment reorganizes presentation without changing canonical content.
The lesson teaches one bounded decision and does not claim to exhaust every jurisdiction, vendor implementation, architecture, attack, or exception.
